source: Forbus, Ferguson, Gentner (1994) Incremental Structure-Mapping (I-SME)
finding: I-SME is SME made incremental. It accepts base and target facts all at once, one at a time, or in any mix, and keeps a small set of global mappings.
numbers: Given all facts at once, I-SME output equals SME output. Cost: greedy merge linear in kernels; kernels between log and linear in match-hypothesis network; network between linear and quadratic in description size. Timing on a PowerBook 165c: toy example 0.5 s, qualitative physics 2 s, two stories of 67 and 52 expressions 34 s.
quote: adding incremental operation does not result in any increase in computational complexity
limits: Only small 1994-era descriptions; no human data of its own.
agent_relevance: S6 can extend a mapping instead of recomputing it; same result as batch matching is a testable invariant.

source: Forbus et al. (1994) I-SME EXTEND step
finding: EXTEND has four steps: add new local match hypotheses against old and new items; update kernels from new root matches downward; score and optionally filter by pragmatics; merge new kernels into the existing mappings.
numbers: Keeps at most n global mappings, all within p% of the best structural score. New hypotheses that break parallel connectivity are marked inconsistent and get nogood links to keep one-to-one.
limits: Greedy merge can lock in early partial matches.
agent_relevance: Keep a few top mappings alive across rounds, not one; mark conflicts explicitly.

source: Forbus et al. (1994) I-SME REMAP step
finding: REMAP clears the global mappings and rebuilds them greedily from all kernels (after optional filtering). It is backtracking at the level of kernels. I-SME does not decide when to remap.
numbers: I-SME reports what fraction of the total possible structural evaluation the current mappings represent, to help an outside controller decide.
quote: we believe remapping criteria tend to be task-specific
limits: Remap trigger left to the task.
agent_relevance: Give S6 a code-computed coverage score (current score over best possible) as the remap trigger, not model opinion (fits G1, G5).

source: Forbus et al. (1994) serial versus parallel design
finding: Local match building and kernel building run in parallel; only the final merge is serial. Fully serial IAM (Keane and Brayshaw 1988) makes local choices one at a time and needs backtracking.
numbers: Authors argue that with large shared systematic structure the number of kernels is small, so serial limited-capacity merging could explain the More-is-Less effect (Gentner and Rattermann 1991).
limits: Psychological plausibility argued, not tested in this paper.
agent_relevance: Cheap parallel candidate generation then a small serial commit step is a good shape for an LLM loop.

source: Forbus et al. (1994) pragmatic filters
finding: Two kernel filters: REQUIRED (externally imposed correspondences, e.g. a speaker says heat is like water) and IDENTICAL-FUNCTIONS (reject root matches pairing non-identical functions).
numbers: In MARS, removing the identical-functions filter let specific enthalpy h match temperature T, giving a simpler but wrong solution. Filters are hard; soft versions were tried.
quote: incremental matching is subject to misleading matches when only partial information is available
limits: Authors say proper filter use may be learned with expertise or metacognitive skill.
agent_relevance: Early partial information misleads mapping; guard S6 with hard type constraints and relax them only on a failed check.

source: Keane (in press, cited in Forbus et al. 1994) order effect in serial attribute mapping
finding: Keane showed that feeding mapping facts one at a time causes order effects: problems whose singleton items come last are harder.
numbers: Singleton-last condition took subjects about twice as long; mean solve time 363.1 s (as quoted by Forbus et al.). Original study not opened.
limits: Second-hand figure; stimuli have no higher-order structure, which Forbus et al. criticise.
agent_relevance: Order of evidence changes the cost of reaching the right mapping; expect order sensitivity in S6.

source: Forbus et al. (1994) I-SME simulation of Keane order effect
finding: I-SME, set to remap whenever an entity or attribute could not be added, reproduces the human order effect.
numbers: Average remaps per example: 1.5 in the easy order, 3.0 in singleton-last, twice as many, matching the roughly twofold human time. Only two example sets shown; no fit statistics.
limits: Uses Keane's own representations; a similarity table was added to match IAM conditions.
agent_relevance: Remap count is a usable difficulty signal for the agent.

source: Forbus et al. (1994) MARS thermodynamics worked-example solver
finding: MARS maps a new thermodynamics problem to a worked example and extends the mapping five times to pull equations and values from candidate inferences. Its solution (Q(h2)=621.22 kW) is correct.
numbers: 16-step solution; five mapping extensions. Representations were built for a tutoring system, not for I-SME. No accuracy rate over a problem set is given.
limits: Single worked demonstration, not a benchmark.
agent_relevance: Closest pattern to S6 across rounds: use a mapping to fetch the next needed piece, then extend.

source: Falkenhainer (1990) Analogy in Context: the map and analyze cycle
finding: PHINEAS-style cycle: make a cheap initial mapping, analyze unmatched parts using the domain theory only where impasses arise, re-examine the mapping (extend or shift), repeat until it cannot be extended.
numbers: Candidate inference check order: already known, then functional analogue believed, then assume if consistent (abductive check), else seek consistent analogues. Consistency of N assumptions must be tested jointly, not one by one.
quote: only when impasses arise ... is the domain theory consulted
limits: Draft paper; examples implemented but not benchmarked on humans.
agent_relevance: Extend on an impasse, and test candidate inferences jointly for consistency before committing.

source: Burstein (1986); Falkenhainer (1987,1990); Keane and Brayshaw (1988) lineage, as told by Forbus et al.
finding: Burstein first modelled incremental analogy; Falkenhainer's PHINEAS used SME in a map/analyze loop; Keane and Brayshaw's IAM was the first general incremental matcher.
numbers: Hummel and Holyoak (1992) also explored incremental mapping but, per Forbus et al., cannot handle higher-order relations.
limits: Lineage as stated by Forbus et al.; originals not opened.
agent_relevance: Incremental mapping is old and well defined; no need to invent a new scheme.

source: Lovett, Gentner, Forbus, Sagi (2006) Simulating time-course phenomena in perceptual similarity via incremental encoding
finding: Early same-different errors reflect attributes encoded before relations, then the mapping is updated incrementally. SME was run on attributes only (short deadline) or attributes then relations with remap (long deadline).
numbers: Goldstone and Medin (1994): deadlines 1, 1.84, 2.68 s; at 1 s two extra matches-in-place (MIPs) and two extra matches-out-of-place (MOPs) raised errors equally; at the long deadline one MIP outweighed two MOPs. Simulation: 1 base scene, 13 comparison scenes, number of SME differences as the measure.
limits: Ordinal fit only. Model misses the large short-versus-long gap at 0 MOPs and the small MOP effect at long deadline in humans.
agent_relevance: Cross-mapped surface matches matter most when evidence is partial; delay commitment until relations are in.

source: Sloutsky and Yarlas (submitted), as reported by Lovett et al. (2006)
finding: Sequential same-different with limited encoding of the base: relational changes were missed far more than attribute changes.
numbers: Base shown 150 ms versus 2100 ms. With ample time d-prime was high in all conditions. With 150 ms, element-mismatch conditions dropped only slightly, relation-only mismatch (E+/R-) dropped sharply. Second-hand; exact d-prime values not read.
limits: Unpublished at the time; numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Relations take longer to encode than attributes; an agent that maps on partial reads will over-trust surface matches.

source: Lovett, Gentner, Forbus, Sagi (2009) Using analogical mapping to simulate time-course phenomena in perceptual similarity
finding: Journal version: encode scenes incrementally from sketches, sample SME output at several stages, replicate three same-different studies.
numbers: Three studies modelled: Goldstone and Medin 1994 (limited time to encode and compare), Sloutsky and Yarlas (limited encoding of base only), Gentner and Sagi 2006 (unlimited time, alignability). A new participant run used heraldic-shield stimuli.
quote: comparison process can operate over incomplete representations
limits: Simple perceptual stimuli; the paper says incremental encoding alone cannot explain every effect.
agent_relevance: Partial-evidence mapping gives orderly, predictable errors, so S6 outputs on partial rounds can be flagged provisional.

source: Lovett and Forbus (2017) Modeling visual problem-solving as analogical reasoning
finding: SME-based Raven's model compares images, reifies the differences and compares those again. When images fail to align it re-encodes and tries again.
numbers: Solved 56/60 Standard Progressive Matrices (75th percentile for American adults); a 54/60 adult sits at the 61st percentile. Sections A to C 12/12, D 10/12, E 10/12. Earlier model got 50/60 (41st percentile).
limits: Hand-tuned qualitative vision pipeline; one test.
agent_relevance: Re-encode then remap on alignment failure is a working recovery move.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat UCLA undergraduates on text matrices, letter strings and verbal analogies, but not on story analogies.
numbers: Digit Matrices: human N=40, GPT-3 above human (generation OR=1.88, p=0.005; multiple choice OR=6.27, p=2.3e-8). Letter strings: human N=57, GPT-3 better overall (OR=1.76, p=6.3e-5). Story analogies: human N=54, humans better (OR=0.37, p=0.0003); GPT-3 not significant in far condition (p=0.065); 15 of 54 people chose the analogous story every trial.
limits: One-shot mapping, no incremental or multi-round test. Later counterfactual tests cut these gains.
agent_relevance: Single-pass mapping by an LLM works on simple relations but is weak on causal structure; story-level mapping needs scaffolding.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Counterfactual tasks for analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Replicating Webb et al. letter strings with permuted alphabets and symbols: GPT models fall sharply, humans stay high.
numbers: Mean accuracy: humans 0.753 (1,876 samples); GPT-3 0.350, GPT-3.5 0.452, GPT-4 0.488 (6,840 samples each; 95% CIs given). Humans stayed flat from 0 to 20 permuted letters; GPT fell. Error type 'alternate rule': GPT-3.5 38.59%, GPT-4 22.00%, GPT-3 5.81%.
limits: Partly a failed replication of generality. Comprehension checks on successor and predecessor were mostly high (0.49 to 1.00), so failure is not only misreading the alphabet.
agent_relevance: Do not trust an LLM's mapping when the surface form is unfamiliar; check on a mutated input (G3).

source: Stevenson et al. (2024) Can LLMs generalize analogy solving like children can?
finding: Letter-string analogies in Latin, Greek (near) and symbols (far): children and adults transfer, LLMs do not.
numbers: Mean accuracy Latin/Greek/Symbol: adults (n=62) 0.88/0.91/0.89; children 7-9 y (n=41) 0.62/0.66/0.67; GPT-4o 0.85/0.63/0.48; Claude-3.5 0.68/0.62/0.46; Llama-3.1 405B 0.79/0.74/0.27; Gemma-2 27B 0.60/0.39/0.14. Each model dropped significantly from Latin to the other alphabets.
limits: Letter strings only. Predecessor and second-successor rules hardest for all.
agent_relevance: Mapping transfers badly to far domains; S6 should expect failure when the target domain shares few surface cues.

source: Hu et al. (2023) In-context analogical reasoning with pre-trained language models
finding: Zero-shot language models solve Raven-style matrices when perceptual features are encoded in text; naming the abstractions helps and grows with model size.
numbers: Accuracies in the text include 77.2% (GPT-3 175B, Center), 78.0% and 86.4% on 2x2 and 3x3 grids. Table layout was garbled in extraction, so column mapping is not verified.
limits: Use as direction only.
agent_relevance: A symbolic, aligned encoding helps an LLM map more than raw text.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Analogical prompting: the model writes its own related problems and knowledge, then solves. It beats 0-shot CoT and often manual few-shot CoT.
numbers: Codeforces Acc@1: GPT-3.5-turbo-16k 15% with self-generated knowledge plus exemplars vs GPT-4 16% (as the paper states). Self-generated exemplars beat retrieved ones at larger scale; retrieved won at smaller scale. Tables 1 and 3 were garbled in extraction, so other numbers are not recorded.
limits: One-shot recall of analogues; no mapping extended across rounds. Gains depend on model scale.
agent_relevance: Self-generated analogues help at scale but give no verified mapping; pair with a code check.

source: Gap check: LLM studies of incremental mapping specifically
finding: I found no LLM study that tests extending or remapping an analogy across rounds as new facts arrive. Search was limited: WebSearch budget exhausted and Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned rate-limit errors.
numbers: Zero dedicated studies found; all LLM studies above are one-shot.
limits: Absence of evidence under a limited search, not proof.
agent_relevance: S6 across rounds is untested for LLMs; treat as [D] and measure ourselves.

source: Forbus, Ferguson, Lovett, Gentner (2016) Extending SME to handle large-scale cognitive modeling
finding: Journal successor of the I-SME paper. The PDF is an image-only scan (21 MB, no text layer) and no OCR tool was available, so I could not read it.
numbers: No numbers extracted.
limits: Unread.
agent_relevance: Read later (needs OCR) for large-scale performance and incremental-mapping results.

source: Cross-link note: sibling subfields
finding: Overlap with structure mapping (01), systematicity (02), candidate inferences (03), retrieval (05) and multiconstraint theory (06) in this folder; I-SME builds on SME of Falkenhainer, Forbus and Gentner (1986, 1989).
numbers: Not a measurement.
limits: Pointer only.
agent_relevance: Do not repeat SME scoring details here.

source: Goldstone and Medin (1994) via Lovett et al. (2009) butterfly same-different
finding: At 1 s, shared attributes raised false 'same' answers whether or not they fit the best alignment. At 1.84 and 2.68 s, cross-mapped (out of place) matches lost most of their effect.
numbers: Deadlines 1, 1.84, 2.68 s within subject; measure: error rate on different trials. Exact error rates not read (second-hand).
limits: Second-hand description.
agent_relevance: With little processing, surface overlap dominates; structure gets weight only with more time, so give S6 enough rounds before judging.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) letter-to-concept generalization
finding: GPT-3 solved letter-string problems that transfer successorship to real-world concepts (e.g. cold cool warm ?), taken as an abstract notion of successor.
numbers: Letter strings: more generalizations lowered accuracy in both humans (OR=0.66 per generalization) and GPT-3 (OR=0.51); error patterns correlated across subtypes r(39)=0.7, p=3.6e-7.
limits: Later counterfactual work (Lewis and Mitchell 2024; Stevenson 2024) shows this does not hold on permuted alphabets or symbols.
agent_relevance: Difficulty rises with the number of rule changes, as with remaps in I-SME.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) comprehension check on altered alphabets
finding: Before the analogy task, models were asked successor and predecessor on permuted alphabets. Most scores were high, but GPT-3 predecessor on permuted pairs with 2 permuted letters was 0.49 on unpermuted items.
numbers: Table 1 cells ranged about 0.49 to 1.00; table layout garbled, so cell labels are approximate.
limits: Approximate reading of a garbled table.
agent_relevance: Check that a mapping's primitive relations are understood before trusting the extended mapping.
